title: Three perfect days in New York, from Midtown's lights to Harlem
dek: The weekend before Thanksgiving, when the rinks are open, the Rockettes are kicking and Brooklyn's botanic garden lights up for winter. Here is how to spend it in Midtown, Prospect Heights and Harlem.

hero.caption: Grand Central's Main Concourse, under its ceiling of painted constellations, on the way down to lunch at the Oyster Bar.

intro:
This is the weekend New York tips into the holidays, and it does so on a schedule. The Christmas Spectacular has been running at Radio City since early November, the Grand Central Holiday Fair is trading in Vanderbilt Hall, and the skating rinks at Bryant Park and Rockefeller Center are open. On Friday night the Brooklyn Botanic Garden switches on **Lightscape**, its winter light trail, for the season; on Saturday the Bronx Zoo's Holiday Lights open to the public. Thanksgiving is the following Thursday, so the city is busy but not yet at full holiday crush: the Saks light show starts Monday and the Rockefeller Center tree is not lit until December 2.

Last week's guide kept to Museum Mile, the Village and the Brooklyn waterfront. This one goes elsewhere. Friday is Midtown at its most classic: the library and Bryant Park, oysters under the vaults of Grand Central, Brancusi at MoMA, and the Rockettes. Saturday crosses to Prospect Heights in Brooklyn, with a farmers market, the park, the Brooklyn Museum's manga show and Lightscape after dark. Sunday starts with smoked fish on the Upper West Side and the American Museum of Natural History, then heads to Harlem for the Studio Museum, which opened its new building on 125th Street a year ago and is free on Sundays.

Late November means short days, with sunset before 4:40 p.m., so the plan puts walks in the morning and the lights at night. AccuWeather's outlook in mid-November called for a sunny, mild Friday; pack a warm layer for the evenings regardless.

days.title: Friday: Midtown, from the library to Radio City
days.intro: A day on foot between 42nd and 50th Streets, with lunch in a train station and a Christmas show at night.

stops.name: Angelina Paris
stops.text: The New York branch of the Paris tearoom faces Bryant Park on Sixth Avenue, and its thick hot chocolate, *l'Africain*, is the right start to a cold-weather weekend. Order a pastry with it, or the full Parisian breakfast if the day is going to be long. Sit by the windows and watch the Winter Village stalls open across the street. Practical note: it opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays; the hot chocolate is rich enough that a small cup is plenty.

stops.name: Bryant Park Winter Village and the New York Public Library
stops.text: Walk through the Bank of America Winter Village while it is quiet, before the rink and the glass-box shops fill up, then cross to the library's Fifth Avenue steps and the stone lions. The Stephen A. Schwarzman Building opens at 10 a.m.; go up to the Rose Main Reading Room, then see the free Polonsky Exhibition of the library's Treasures, which covers some 4,000 years of books and objects. Practical note: the library has a free self-guided audio tour on the Bloomberg Connects app.
stops.wiki: New York Public Library Main Branch

stops.name: Grand Central Oyster Bar
stops.text: Walk east on 42nd Street to Grand Central, look up at the constellations on the Main Concourse ceiling, and then go down the ramps to the Oyster Bar under its tiled vaults. Sit at the counter and order a dozen oysters from the long daily list and a pan roast, cooked to order in front of you. On the way out, stand in a corner of the arched Whispering Gallery outside the door and talk to the wall. Practical note: the Oyster Bar is open weekdays only, from 11:30 a.m., so Friday is your day; the Holiday Fair in Vanderbilt Hall opens at 10 a.m.

stops.name: Museum of Modern Art: Brancusi
stops.text: MoMA's big autumn show, *Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio*, runs to February 27 and treats the Romanian sculptor's Paris studio as a work in itself, with drawings, photographs, films, tools and even records he owned alongside the sculpture. Hyperallergic's critic admired the art and grumbled about the galleries, so go early in the afternoon before the after-work crowd. Then use the rest of the ticket on the collection floors or the new *Nilima Sheikh: Fractured Skies*. Practical note: buy a timed ticket online to skip the line on 53rd Street.

stops.name: Rockefeller Center and the Rink
stops.text: Walk two blocks to Rockefeller Center as the light goes. The tree is not lit until December 2, but the Channel Gardens, the flags and the gold Prometheus over the rink are all there, and skating at dusk below the towers is the most New York thing you can do in a pair of rented blades. Sessions are timed, about an hour long, and general skate starts at $22. Practical note: book a slot ahead, since Friday evenings sell out.

stops.name: Christmas Spectacular Starring the Radio City Rockettes
stops.text: Radio City Music Hall, the Art Deco hall at Sixth Avenue and 50th Street, is half the reason to go. The 2026 edition runs 230 performances through January 4, with a new number added to fan favorites like the Parade of the Wooden Soldiers. It is unashamedly sentimental, precise and about 90 minutes long, which leaves room for a late dinner. Practical note: there are several shows a day on weekends; check the evening times when you book, and tickets bought at the box office start a little lower than online.

stops.name: Keens Steakhouse
stops.text: Keens has served its mutton chop since the 19th century, and it is still the order: a two-inch-thick cut with mint jelly. The rooms are dark wood and old playbills, and about 45,000 clay churchwarden pipes line the ceilings, each once kept for a regular. If you are not hungry enough for the chop, eat at the pub room with the prime rib hash and a martini. Practical note: it is open until 10:30 p.m. on Fridays; reserve through its website, though the bar takes walk-ins.

days.title: Saturday: Prospect Heights and the park
days.intro: Brooklyn's other side of the park: market, museum, a long walk and the botanic garden lit up after dark.

stops.name: Tom's Restaurant
stops.text: Tom's has been on Washington Avenue since the 1930s, and the weekend line is part of it. Expect a crowded, old-fashioned room and griddle breakfasts: pancakes, eggs, and coffee refilled without asking. It opens at 7 a.m., so get there early and you will be eating within minutes. Practical note: it is a short walk from the Brooklyn Museum stop on the 2 and 3 trains.

stops.name: Grand Army Plaza Greenmarket and the Long Meadow
stops.text: Walk to Grand Army Plaza and the arch, then into the Saturday Greenmarket at the park's northwest entrance, where regional farms sell late-season produce, cider and baked goods. From there, go into Prospect Park and along the Long Meadow, the long, rolling lawn that Olmsted and Vaux laid out as the park's centerpiece. Practical note: the market runs every Saturday; bring cash for smaller stands.
stops.addr: Prospect Park West and Flatbush Avenue

stops.name: Brooklyn Museum
stops.text: The museum's fall season is its strongest in years. *Art of Manga*, in the Great Hall to January 31, makes its East Coast debut with original pages from *One Piece*, *JoJo's Bizarre Adventure* and *Inuyasha*, paired with *Manga Before Manga*, older Japanese art from the collection. *Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses*, the Dutch designer's couture, closes December 6, so this is one of its last weekends. Practical note: it opens at 11 a.m. Wednesday to Sunday and is closed Monday and Tuesday.

stops.name: Cafe Mado
stops.text: A coffee counter up front and a skylit dining room behind, a few minutes from the museum on Washington Avenue. At lunch it sells house-baked bread, breakfast sandwiches and handmade pasta; the Infatuation's pick is the Tony, a mortadella sandwich. Michelin's inspectors note the pici with pesto Genovese. Practical note: weekend daytime service runs 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m., so don't linger too long in the museum.

stops.name: Sofreh
stops.text: Nasim Alikhani's Persian restaurant on a quiet corner off Flatbush is the best dinner in the neighborhood for a cold night. Order the smoky roasted eggplant, the lamb shank in a dill and dried-lime broth, and the saffron rice, and share everything. The room is warm and low-lit, and solo diners do well at the bar. Practical note: book the earliest seating, and pick a Lightscape entry window about two hours later.

stops.name: Lightscape at Brooklyn Botanic Garden
stops.text: The winter light trail opened Friday for its run to January 3, with a new trail this year alongside favorites like the Cathedral Tunnel and work by local artists, laid out along a trail of about a million lights through the garden after dark. Practical note: tickets are timed in 15-minute windows and sold online or by phone through the Garden's ticketing partner, Leap; adult prices run $29 to $44 by night, and popular dates sell out. The trail starts at the Visitor Center on Washington Avenue.

stops.name: Grimm Tavern
stops.text: Grimm Artisanal Ales, one of Brooklyn's best breweries, opened this tavern in June in the old Olmsted space on Vanderbilt Avenue, keeping the plant wall and the heated covered backyard. There are 20 taps of Grimm's IPAs, sours and stouts. Have a beer with the soft pretzel and horseradish sauce, the dish both Time Out and the Infatuation singled out. Practical note: it is open until midnight Tuesday to Saturday and closed Sunday and Monday.

days.title: Sunday: the Upper West Side to Harlem
days.intro: Smoked fish and dinosaurs in the morning, then uptown to 125th Street for art and Harlem's two best-known dining rooms.

stops.name: Barney Greengrass
stops.text: The self-styled Sturgeon King has been selling smoked fish on Amsterdam Avenue since 1908, and the dining room has not tried to look any younger. Order eggs scrambled with lox and onions, or a sturgeon or sable sandwich on rye. It is pricey and fills up as the morning goes on, which is why you are here at 9. Practical note: no reservations, closed Mondays; the restaurant opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekends.

stops.name: American Museum of Natural History
stops.text: Enter through the Gilder Center on Columbus Avenue, a canyon of curving concrete that is worth the trip alone, and go straight up to the fourth-floor dinosaur halls while they are quiet. Then see the blue whale in the Hall of Ocean Life. *Apex*, the Stegosaurus fossil, is included in general admission; the butterfly vivarium and planetarium show cost extra. Practical note: it opens at 10 a.m. daily; New York State residents pay what they wish for general admission.

stops.name: Red Rooster
stops.text: Take the B or C train up to 125th Street and walk east to Lenox Avenue. Marcus Samuelsson's restaurant has anchored this stretch of the avenue since 2010, mixing Southern cooking with his Swedish and Ethiopian roots. Sunday is the day for it: the dining room opens at 10 a.m. and runs through the afternoon. Order the fried chicken, share a few sides, and leave room for the walk. Practical note: book ahead on weekends.

stops.name: Studio Museum in Harlem
stops.text: The Studio Museum opened its new building on West 125th Street in November 2025, after seven years away, and it is free every Sunday. This fall's shows include *Dreams of This Future*, drawn from Peggy Cooper Cafritz's bequest of work by artists of African descent; *Tone*, a nineteen-artist group show; and the 2026 artists in residence. Look for Camille Norment's installation and Christopher Myers's *Harlem Is a Myth*. Practical note: Sunday hours are 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.; you can book tickets online ahead.

stops.name: 125th Street to Strivers' Row
stops.text: Walk west a block to see the Apollo's marquee, then north up Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard to Strivers' Row on West 138th and 139th Streets, where the 1890s rowhouses by McKim, Mead & White and others still have their alleys signed *Walk Your Horses*. It is about 20 minutes each way and best in the last light. Practical note: these are private homes; keep to the sidewalk.

stops.name: Sylvia's
stops.text: Sylvia Woods opened her restaurant on Lenox Avenue in 1962, and it has fed Harlem and its visitors ever since. Red Rooster is the modern version; this is the original. Keep it simple: smothered chicken or barbecue ribs with collards and candied yams, then peach cobbler. Practical note: it closes at 8 p.m. on Sundays, and it does not book through OpenTable; call ahead for larger groups.

stops.name: Knicks vs. Indiana Pacers
stops.text: If you have energy left, the 2 and 3 trains run from 125th Street straight to Penn Station and Madison Square Garden, where the Knicks host the Pacers at 8 p.m., a rematch of recent playoff series. A Sunday night game at the Garden is the city at its loudest. Practical note: buy through the Garden's own site or a verified resale platform, and expect the 2 and 3 to be full after the game.

stay.name: The Peninsula New York
stay.text: A 1905 Beaux-Arts building at Fifth Avenue and 55th Street, renovated in 2024, with a 22nd-floor indoor pool and the Pen Top rooftop bar. It puts you a few minutes' walk from MoMA, Rockefeller Center and the Fifth Avenue windows, which matters on a holiday weekend.

stay.name: The Algonquin Hotel
stay.text: The Round Table's old hotel, refreshed this year with redone rooms and Al Hirschfeld artwork chosen with his foundation. It is a short walk from Bryant Park, Grand Central and Radio City, so Friday's plan needs no subway at all.

stay.name: Arlo Midtown
stay.text: Small, well-designed rooms with big windows on West 38th Street, about ten minutes on foot from Penn Station, which makes the airport trains and the Sunday Knicks game easy. Rooms are compact; ask for a high floor.

events.name: Lightscape opens at Brooklyn Botanic Garden
events.when: Fri. evening, timed entry; through Jan. 3
events.where: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, 990 Washington Avenue, Brooklyn
events.text: The winter light trail returns for its season with a new trail. Tickets are timed and sold online; the garden closes to day visitors at 3:30 p.m. on event days.

events.name: Juilliard at the Apollo: Kind of Blue
events.where: The Apollo Stages at the Victoria, 233 W. 125th Street
events.text: Juilliard Jazz and the Apollo mark Miles Davis's centennial with a performance built around *Kind of Blue*. Tickets are $25; a preconcert talk precedes Friday's show.

events.name: Bronx Zoo Holiday Lights opens
events.when: Sat. from 1 p.m.; lights on 4:30 p.m., last entry 8 p.m.
events.text: The zoo's lantern festival opens to the public, this year with evening access to the Children's Zoo farmyard, World of Darkness and World of Reptiles. Advance tickets only.

events.name: Knicks vs. Portland Trail Blazers
events.text: The first of two Knicks home games this weekend.

events.name: Knicks vs. Indiana Pacers
events.text: Sunday night at the Garden; expect crowds at Penn Station before and after.

events.name: Saks Fifth Avenue holiday light show begins
events.where: Saks Fifth Avenue, Fifth Avenue at 50th Street
events.text: The light show returns to the store's façade on Monday; if you are staying an extra night, it is across the street from St. Patrick's and a block from Rockefeller Center.

know: **From the airports.** From JFK, take the AirTrain to Jamaica and change to the subway or the Long Island Rail Road; the AirTrain is a separate fare. Allow about an hour to Midtown. From Newark, the AirTrain connects to NJ Transit trains to Penn Station, From LaGuardia, the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus runs to the subway at Jackson Heights. Taxis from JFK to Manhattan charge a flat fare plus tolls, surcharges and tip.

**Paying for transit.** Tap a contactless card or phone at subway turnstiles and on buses with OMNY. A ride is $3, and once one card has paid for $34 of rides in a Monday-to-Sunday week, the rest of that week's rides are free. Use one card per person.

**Thanksgiving week.** The holiday is Thursday, November 26, with the Macy's parade that morning and balloon inflation on the Upper West Side on Wednesday the 25th. This weekend is busy but not yet peak; Fifth Avenue between 49th and 59th Streets gets crowded in the evenings once the Saks show starts on Monday.

**Closed days.** The Brooklyn Museum is closed Monday and Tuesday and the Studio Museum Monday and Tuesday; Barney Greengrass is closed Mondays; Grimm Tavern is closed Sunday and Monday. The Grand Central Oyster Bar serves weekdays only, and Keens opens for dinner only on weekends.

**Crowds and transit.** The Knicks play Madison Square Garden on Saturday at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday at 8 p.m., so Penn Station and the trains through it will be busy those nights. Check the MTA's weekend service changes before you travel, since weekend track work often reroutes lines.

**The weather and the light.** AccuWeather's mid-November outlook called for a sunny, mild Friday, with highs around 60°F. Sunset is about 4:35 p.m., so do the walks early and save the lights for after dark.
**Tipping.** In restaurants, 18 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill is normal; at bars, a dollar or two a drink; for taxis, 15 to 20 percent.
